Most of us have been using AI in single-player mode, where your AI OS, skills, and connected accounts only help you. 

In this video I show how my team and I use Kylon to put humans and agents in one shared workspace, including our own Claude Code and Codex subscriptions, so everyone can build apps and automations together. I also walk through a fresh setup, how credits and pricing work, and how I’d roll this out to a team one work stream at a time. Kylon sponsored this video.

The multiplayer shift is real, and the coordination part is where we have bled the most. We once ran a researcher agent plus a writer agent for a client, and the researcher kept overwriting the writer's drafts because nobody owned the shared doc. Now we give one agent the pen and the other one read-only access, and everything gets calmer. The orchestration pattern matters more than the model :)

Multiplayer is where the hidden bill shows up: every extra agent adds handoffs, not just hands. We ran 40 Claude Code agents and cut to 15 because coordination was eating more than the parallelism gave back. Fewer agents, written handoffs and one reviewer per gate is what actually scaled.

On the 14:30 point about local agents going offline: if you go the Mac mini or plugged-in laptop route, run `caffeinate -s` in Terminal (built into macOS) or turn on "prevent automatic sleeping" in Energy settings, otherwise the machine still sleeps and your teammates get silence. Also curious: when a teammate messages your local Claude Code, does it inherit your env vars and connected accounts, or can you scope what it can touch per channel?
